reach: In the culture of The Reach, chivalry, beauty, and courtly grace are prized above all else. House Tyrell sets the tone for the entire region — romance is celebrated openly, and the giving of flowers, especially roses, is a deeply ingrained tradition. Suitors are expected to compose poetry, sing songs, and demonstrate their refinement through wit and charm rather than brute strength. Formal courtship is important, and the approval of the family is essential. However, the Reach also has a romantic and idealistic streak — genuine love is celebrated here more than in most of Westeros. A person of the Reach believes that beauty and grace in a partner are as important as political advantage.
vlandia: In Westerlands culture, wealth, power, and the Lannister legacy dominate everything — including romance. A Lannister always pays their debts, and this extends to romantic obligations. Marriages are arrangements of power and gold first, love second. A suitor must demonstrate their worth through resources, political connections, or military strength. Displays of lavish generosity — expensive gifts, grand feasts, tokens of gold — are expected forms of courtship. However, a Westerlands noble who genuinely falls in love will pursue it with the same calculating ruthlessness they apply to everything, making them unexpectedly devoted partners once their heart is truly won.
battania: In the culture of the North, honor, loyalty, and the Old Gods come before all else. The Northerners are a stoic people — they do not express affection through flowery words or grand courtly gestures. Instead, they show love through steadfast loyalty, protection, and enduring hardship together. Standing by someone when the world turns against them is the highest romantic gesture a Northerner knows. The approval of the family and the lords of Winterfell matters deeply. Northerners do not forget a betrayal, and they do not forgive it easily — but once their loyalty is given, it is given for life.
sturgia: In Iron Islands culture, strength, self-reliance, and the Iron Price define everything — including romance. The Ironborn take what they want rather than buying it, and their approach to courtship reflects this directness. They are not given to soft words, poetry, or courtly gestures — they show affection through fierce protectiveness, loyalty in battle, and sharing the hardship of the sea. An Ironborn respects strength above all else, and a partner who can match their ferocity and independence is prized. The Drowned God demands sacrifice, and the Ironborn understand that love, like everything else, comes at a cost.
aserai: In Dornish culture, passion, equality, and personal freedom in matters of love set Dorne apart from the rest of Westeros. Dorne has far more liberal attitudes toward romance — love outside of marriage is more accepted, and women hold considerably more power and agency. A Dornishman or Dornishwoman values intensity, directness, and mutual desire above social convention. They do not hide their feelings, and they expect the same honesty in return. Displays of passion and personal devotion matter far more than formal ceremony. The Martells rule by the words 'Unbowed, Unbent, Unbroken' — and their people are equally unyielding in love.
khuzait: Among the Dothraki, strength, courage, and dominance are everything. The Dothraki do not court — they take. A khal proves his worth through conquest and the size of his khalasar. A partner is won through displays of extraordinary martial prowess, horse riding, and combat. The Dothraki have little use for the soft customs of the settled world — love among them is fierce, physical, and tied to power. A Dothraki who chooses a partner considers it a statement of strength, not sentiment. Respect must be earned and demonstrated continuously. Weakness of any kind is despised.
nightswatch: The Night's Watch takes no wives and holds no lands — their vows forbid romantic attachment entirely. Those who wear the black have sworn themselves to celibacy and service at the Wall. However, human nature does not die with a vow, and rangers who have ranged far from Castle Black have been known to form deep bonds. For those of Night's Watch culture who pursue romance regardless of their vows, it is done in absolute secrecy and with the constant shadow of guilt and duty. Such connections are intense, brief, and often tragic — shaped entirely by the knowledge that the Wall comes first.
vale: In the culture of the Vale, honor, tradition, and the isolation of the Eyrie shape romantic life profoundly. The Vale is a proud and insular region, and romantic relationships among the nobility require adherence to strict social norms and the approval of the Lord of the Eyrie. The Arryns prize purity of character, chivalric conduct, and loyalty above all. Suitors must demonstrate their honor through formal courtship — a proper approach to the family, gifts appropriate to station, and a demonstrated willingness to protect and serve. The Vale's isolation has made its nobility somewhat suspicious of outsiders, and winning the trust of a Vale noble takes considerable patience.
river: In Riverlands culture, the words of House Tully — Family, Duty, Honor — define all aspects of life, including love. The Riverlands have suffered more war and occupation than almost any other region of Westeros, and this has made its people value stability, loyalty, and family bonds intensely. Romantic relationships must align with family interests and earn the blessing of the lord of the house. A formal courtship, the approval of elders, and a demonstrated commitment to duty are expected. Yet beneath the formality, the people of the Riverlands are warm-hearted and feel love deeply — they simply know that love alone cannot protect a family from the storms of war.
dragonstone: In Dragonstone culture, shaped by the legacy of House Targaryen, blood and lineage are sacred. Historically, Targaryens married within the family to keep the dragonlord bloodline pure — though this tradition has become rarer. In romantic relationships, Targaryen-influenced culture values passion, intensity, and a certain grandiosity. They love fiercely or not at all. Fire and blood run in their veins, and their emotions reflect this extremity. A Targaryen or Dragonstone noble is drawn to those who see them as a person rather than a symbol, and they prize fierce, unconditional loyalty above all else.
stormlands: In Stormlands culture, shaped by House Baratheon, strength, fierce passion, and decisive action are the defining traits. The storms that batter their coastline mirror the temperament of their people — powerful, unpredictable, and unrelenting. In romantic relationships, they value partners who can match their energy and intensity. They are direct — a Stormlander says what they mean and does what they say. Grand gestures of strength or courage, fierce protectiveness of loved ones, and a refusal to back down are all signs of deep affection. They do not do anything halfway, including love.
crownlands: In the Crownlands, shaped by King's Landing and proximity to the Iron Throne, political calculation and social sophistication define romantic life. Those who live in the shadow of the throne understand that every relationship has political dimensions. Courtship here is a careful game of social positioning — public displays of affection are managed carefully, alliances through marriage are common, and genuine love is often a luxury of the lower classes. Yet the smallfolk of the Crownlands, removed from the politics of the great houses, form bonds as genuine and simple as anywhere in Westeros.
ghiscari: In Ghiscari culture, shaped by the ancient traditions of Slaver's Bay and the cities of Astapor, Yunkai, and Meereen, social hierarchy and the rigid structure of the old slave cities dominate romantic life. Among the Great Masters, marriage is a matter of status and the preservation of ancient lineages. Courtship follows elaborate formal rituals reflecting one's position in the social hierarchy. However, since the liberation of Slaver's Bay, new attitudes toward love and freedom have begun to take hold among the formerly enslaved — love freely chosen, rather than arranged, has become a powerful symbol of liberation.
freefolk: Among the Free Folk beyond the Wall, known to southerners as wildlings, love and partnership are remarkably direct. The Free Folk recognize no lords, no kings, and no social hierarchies — and this extends to romance. A woman 'steals' a man she wants by capturing him, proving she is strong enough to take what she desires. A man who is stolen considers it a compliment — only someone worth having is worth stealing. Free Folk relationships are built on mutual strength and respect. Weakness is not tolerated, but genuine partnership between equals is deeply valued. They are not bound by the southern customs of formal courtship or family approval.
norvos: In Norvoshi culture, the bearded priests of Norvos hold great influence over all aspects of life, including romance. Courtship follows strict religious traditions overseen by the city's clergy. The sacred bells of Norvos ring to mark important life events including betrothals and unions. Norvoshi value discipline, devotion to their gods, and a strong sense of civic duty. A romantic partner must be approved through religious as well as social channels. However, the lower city of Norvos, home to the axe-wielding sellswords and common folk, has more relaxed attitudes — direct, practical, and shaped by the rough life of mercenary work.
valyrian: In Valyrian culture, shaped by the memory of the great Freehold and its dragon lords, blood purity, sorcerous power, and ancient lineage define romantic life. The Valyrians practiced endogamy — marriage within the family — to preserve dragonlord blood. True Valyrian culture is largely extinct since the Doom of Valyria, but those who carry Valyrian heritage prize it intensely. Romance among those of Valyrian descent carries the weight of history and loss — the last embers of a civilization that once ruled the world. Passion, intellect, and the mystical connection to dragons and fire are deeply romantic ideals in this tradition.
volantine: In Volantene culture, one of the wealthiest and most powerful of the Free Cities, a rigid triarchy of noble families rules everything. Old Blood families — those who can trace their lineage to Valyria — control politics, commerce, and social life. Romantic relationships among the Old Blood are tightly regulated by family and political alliance. Elaborate face tattoos mark the enslaved population of Volantis, and the distinction between slave and free is absolute. Among the Old Blood, courtship is formal, politically calculated, and tied to the preservation of ancient lineages. Among the common folk and freed slaves, romance is far more openly expressed.
empire: In Braavosi culture, independence, skill, and self-determination are the supreme values. Braavos was founded by escaped slaves who swore never to keep slaves, and this history of freedom permeates every aspect of Braavosi life. The Sealord of Braavos rules a city of canals, commerce, and the mysterious Faceless Men. In romance, Braavosi value personal freedom and mutual choice above family obligation or political arrangement. The Braavosi are known for their dueling culture — a suitor might prove their worth through skill with a blade. The courtesans of Braavos are legendary throughout the known world, and romance in this city is treated as an art form.
nord: In Nord culture, honor, personal prowess, and a strong connection to the sea are valued. In romantic relationships, proofs of bravery and skill are expected — victory in a naval raid, crafting a fine weapon as a gift, or demonstrating seamanship. They value straightforwardness in speech and actions, as well as fierce loyalty to one's kin and chosen partner. A Nord who gives their word keeps it, and they expect the same in return. Betrayal is the gravest sin in Nord culture, and it is never forgotten.
pentoshi: In Pentoshi culture, wealth, refinement, and the pleasures of civilized life define romantic ideals. Pentos is a city of wealthy magisters and lush gardens, where comfort and luxury are prized. Romantic courtship here is gentle and sophisticated — gifts of fine food and wine, invitations to garden parties, the exchange of poetry and music. The Pentoshi are not a martial people; they prefer to hire sellswords to fight their wars and focus their energies on commerce and pleasure. A romantic partner in Pentoshi culture is expected to be cultured, witty, and capable of enjoying the finer things in life.
myrish: In Myrish culture, famous for its fine lace, intricate lenses, and skilled craftspeople, attention to detail and craftsmanship are considered romantic virtues. Myr is a city of artisans, and a suitor might demonstrate their affection through a beautifully crafted gift — a piece of fine lace, a pair of Myrish lenses, or an intricate mechanical device. The Myrish value intelligence, skill, and patience. Romantic relationships here tend to develop slowly and carefully, like the intricate work for which the city is famous. The Myrish are also known for their carpets and tapestries, and the telling of stories — a well-told tale is considered a deeply romantic gesture.
lyseni: In Lyseni culture, beauty, pleasure, and the art of love are elevated to a near-sacred status. Lys is famous throughout the known world for its pleasure houses and its beautiful, silver-haired inhabitants — many of whom carry Valyrian blood. In romance, the Lyseni value physical beauty, grace, and the sophisticated art of seduction. Love potions are said to originate from Lys. Romantic gestures here are sensual and elaborate — perfumed oils, silk garments, music, and dance. The Lyseni are direct about desire and consider the concealment of attraction somewhat dishonest. However, beneath the surface, the Lyseni also value genuine emotional connection — they simply believe it should be expressed beautifully.
tyroshi: In Tyroshi culture, flamboyance, commerce, and competitive one-upmanship define the character of the city. The Tyroshi are known for their brightly dyed beards, their love of gaudy display, and their cutthroat mercantile spirit. In romantic relationships, they value bold displays of wealth and personality — a Tyroshi suitor will arrive in the most colorful clothes, with the most expensive gifts, determined to outshine all rivals. The Tyroshi are competitive in everything, including love, and they pursue romantic partners with the same aggressive enthusiasm they apply to business negotiations. Underneath the showmanship, however, the Tyroshi are passionately loyal to those who have truly won their heart.
skagosi: In Skagosi culture, from the remote and forbidding island of Skagos in the Bay of Seals, strength and survival in harsh conditions are the defining values. The Skagosi are an ancient, isolated people who still ride unicorns and are rumored by mainlanders to practice cannibalism — though the truth of this is uncertain. In romance, the Skagosi value raw physical strength, endurance, and the ability to survive the brutal conditions of their island. A suitor must prove they are capable of protecting their partner and providing in a land where survival is never guaranteed. Skagosi romantic traditions are ancient, largely unknown to the wider world, and shaped entirely by the demands of life on a remote and unforgiving island.
sarnor: In Sarnori culture — the remnants of the once-great Kingdom of the Sarnori, the Tall Men of the grasslands — pride in ancient heritage and the memory of lost greatness shape romantic ideals. The Sarnori cities were largely destroyed by the Dothraki, and the surviving Sarnori carry deep wounds of cultural loss. In romance, they value intelligence, learning, and the preservation of their ancient traditions. A partner who respects and shares in the remembrance of Sarnori history and culture is deeply prized. There is also a tragic romanticism to Sarnori culture — love shadowed by loss, beauty persisting in the face of destruction.
yiti: In Yi Tish culture, from the ancient and mysterious empire of Yi Ti in the far east of the known world, elaborate ceremony, ancestral tradition, and the divine authority of the God-Emperor shape all aspects of life. Yi Ti is one of the oldest civilizations in the known world, and its romantic traditions are ancient and highly formalized. Courtship involves elaborate rituals, the exchange of gifts with deep symbolic meaning, and the approval of extended family and community elders. Beauty, wisdom, and refined conduct are prized in a partner. Yi Tish culture values harmony and the proper ordering of relationships within the greater social fabric.
summer: In Summer Islands culture, from the beautiful tropical islands far to the south, love and physical intimacy are celebrated openly and joyfully as gifts from the gods. The Summer Islanders worship a goddess of love and beauty, and they consider the open expression of desire to be a form of prayer. Romance here is warm, generous, and uninhibited by the guilt or shame found in other cultures. The Summer Islanders are skilled sailors and traders, and their attitude toward love reflects their relationship with the sea — open, generous, and filled with wonder. A Summer Islander will express their feelings directly and joyfully, expecting the same openness in return.
whitewalker: The White Walkers are ancient, inhuman beings of ice and death from beyond the Wall. They do not experience love or romance as mortals understand it. Their existence is defined entirely by cold, death, and the raising of the dead. Any interaction with a White Walker is one of absolute existential threat — they do not court, they do not feel, they do not connect. They are the end of all warmth.
